findings.passage: He was answering a leading question and speaking in the second person. He named two routes to earned love, charm or achievement, without saying which was his.
findings.problem: This misdescribes the Playboy text (S03, reopened for this review). Straight after "you can get very good at trying to earn the love of others" he says "Bill Clinton is like me in that regard," in the first person. When Sheff then asks "Do the achievements fill the void?" he answers "Yes and no" and tells the sister story as his own answer, ending "Of course she's right." He places himself in the passage and accepts the premise that his achievements were aimed at the void. The draft itself reports the Clinton and Churchill comparison two paragraphs earlier, so the page contradicts itself. One of the two stated reasons Type 8 stays ahead rests on a misreading of the best-known Type 3 evidence.
findings.acceptance_test: The paragraph no longer says he spoke only in the second person or that he did not say which route was his. It reports "Bill Clinton is like me in that regard" and the "Yes and no" answer to "Do the achievements fill the void?". Any discount that remains (a leading question, a retrospective answer) is one the S03 text supports. If none remains, the paragraph is cut and the section says the passage counts for Type 3 at face value.

findings.passage: The man who calls "questioning authority" the core of his character has spent more than two decades arguing that the state should watch more.
findings.problem: Two facts in the draft's own opened sources are missing, and both change this section. (a) In the 1997 Academy interview (S02), the answer that supplies "questioning authority" also says what he was questioning: his adoptive father "loved our government as only an immigrant can," held to "my country, right or wrong," "never questioned the government's policies," and Ellison mocks the belief that "The government knows everything." By 2002 he is saying "I would rather trust our government." The contradiction is sharper than authority in general: he ended up close to the view he says he defined himself against. "What Ellison has resisted since childhood is authority over him" does not answer that. (b) Oracle was named for a CIA project and the CIA was among its first customers (Academy biography S27; Fortune S07). His tie to state intelligence dates from 1977, so "more than two decades" and "22 years of consistency" start the clock 25 years late, and McAllister's commercial objection is stronger than "a key Oracle market" suggests.
findings.acceptance_test: The section (i) reports the father-and-government passage from S02 and says plainly that his 2002 to 2024 statements sit near the position he says he rebelled against; (ii) states, sourced to S27 or S07, that Oracle took its name from CIA work and counted the CIA as an early customer, placed beside McAllister's objection; (iii) no longer presents 2002 as the start of his alignment with state surveillance. The type reading is then offered beside the commercial one, and the sentence "Read through the type, the contradiction shrinks" is kept only if it still holds after (i) and (ii).

findings.passage: "It's not terribly fashionable to be a supporter of Michael Milken, but I'm honored to have him as my friend," he said.
findings.problem: Ellison co-founded Milken's education company Knowledge Universe in 1996, the year before this interview, with a reported $250 million investment. I checked this only against Wikipedia, which cites Forbes (2001) and CNN Money (2004); it is not in the evidence record and needs an opened source. If confirmed, the remark is a defense of a current business partner, and the same answer (S02) goes further than the draft shows: he says Milken was jailed "because of someone's political advantage." The bullet presents the remark as an unprompted loyalty that cost him approval, the hedge "a wealthy, well-connected ally" undersells a quarter-billion-dollar joint venture, and the evidence record's note that it "gains nothing obvious" (C17) would be wrong.
findings.acceptance_test: The editor checks the Knowledge Universe partnership in an opened source. If confirmed, the page names it where the Milken remark is used or in the "second reading" paragraph, and the remark is no longer counted as a case where approval was the only thing at stake. If it cannot be confirmed, the resolution records the attempt and the current hedge stays.

findings.passage: The Type 3 case is strong, and most of it comes from Ellison.
findings.problem: The section leaves out the best-known Type 3 evidence: his long public fixation on outranking Bill Gates and Microsoft. Fortune's 2000 profile (S07), the source of the "Rosebud" line, says passing Gates as the richest man "may matter even more to Ellison" than Oracle's dominance, and Jobs's joke answers that very paragraph. In Playboy (S03) he says "what really means a lot to me is Oracle passing Microsoft" and "It's hard to go from number two to number one." The evidence record lists the Gates race under evidence against Type 8, yet the draft uses the rivalry only as scenery in the opening, and "He does not say he wanted to be rich, or first, or famous" stands with no mention of his later record on rank. The alternative is being tested below full strength.
findings.acceptance_test: The Why-not-Type-3 section includes the rank evidence with at least one sourced quotation from S03 or S07 and says how the Type 8 reading handles it, or that it does not. The "rich, or first, or famous" sentence is limited in so many words to his account of why he founded the company.

findings.passage: It is the trash press conference at a different scale: a public doubt about his word, answered with force and no explanation.
findings.problem: The obvious precedent for an Ellison-backed hostile bid is Oracle's hostile takeover of PeopleSoft, the largest fight of his business career, and the page never mentions it. The Academy biography (S27) records the purchase at the end of 2004 for $10.3 billion. CBS (S04) presents his "personal vanity" admission as his answer about that takeover, which it says "will potentially put thousands of people out of work"; the draft quotes the admission without that context. The Playboy introduction (S03) quotes PeopleSoft's chief Craig Conway on him. `knows_about` lists "Corporate acquisitions" while the body covers none. From memory, not verified here: the bid opened in June 2003, survived a Justice Department antitrust suit, and was followed by about 5,000 layoffs in January 2005. Those details need an opened source, and they belong in "What the control costs other people" if used.
findings.acceptance_test: The page states the PeopleSoft hostile bid with its dates and outcome from an opened source and places the "personal vanity" quotation in its takeover context. Job-cut figures appear only with an opened source. The December 2025 guarantee is compared with PeopleSoft at least as directly as with the trash press conference. Net body length stays inside the release limit.

findings.passage: It also reads as an accurate self-portrait: a man who met a real limit, respected it, and still left himself an opening.
findings.problem: The section stops before the most famous part of his sailing life. After Hobart he turned to the America's Cup. The Playboy introduction (S03) says "Ellison is going back for more," and in the same exchange as the vow he answers "Absolutely" when asked if the storm made him more cautious. The Academy biography (S27) records the 2010 win, the 2013 defense held in San Francisco Bay "At Ellison's insistence," and the comeback from eight races down. The body never mentions the Cup, although `knows_about` lists "America's Cup sailing." The omission costs the page evidence for its own thesis (he moved to a contest where the holder sets the venue and terms) and hides an adverse side an informed reader will know: Oracle Team USA's 2013 penalty for illegal boat modifications and the death of Artemis sailor Andrew Simpson in the boat class chosen for that Cup. Both are from memory and not verified here.
findings.acceptance_test: The section or the next one says, with sources (S03 and S27 at minimum), what he did after 1998: that the storm made him more cautious by his own account and that he went on to pursue and win the America's Cup in 2010 and 2013. Whether he ever sailed Sydney to Hobart again is stated only if sourced. The 2013 penalty appears only with an opened source and the jury's finding stated plainly; if it is left out, the resolution says why. Body and `knows_about` agree.

findings.passage: He left two universities without a degree, drove to California and taught himself to program.
findings.problem: Formative facts in the opened sources are missing. The Academy biography (S27) says his adoptive mother died during his second-year finals at Illinois and he left. CBS (S04) says his father told him at 12 that he was adopted and quotes him: "It was shocking that I just put it away and thought about it for years." Fortune (S07) says he met his birth mother only once. Followed directly by "lousy student," the dropout reads as plain academic failure. The gap matters later too: the page treats a six-year-old's fear that his mother would not come home as the only deep fear he admits, the same interview calls her the supportive parent ("my Mom was supportive"), and the reader is never told she died when he was about twenty.
findings.acceptance_test: The page states, with sources and no causal claim, that his adoptive mother died during his second year at Illinois and that he left, and that he learned at 12 he was adopted. The six-year-old memory makes clear it concerns his adoptive mother. The restraint of "It is better left unexplained" stays.

findings.passage: Jobs did not explain the joke.
findings.problem: Jobs appears only as this punchline and in the HP email, yet the speech the draft already cites (S05) holds the best-known story in which Ellison gives up control. In mid-1995 at Castle Rock he had, by his account, arranged the money to buy Apple and install Jobs as chief executive. Jobs refused, and Ellison says he told him, "It's your company and it's your call. I'll do whatever you want me to do." It is a counter-instance to "he repeatedly takes control," and the only close relationship in the record that is not with a rival or an ousted executive, a skew the research notes admit. It was held back as single-source, but most of the page rests on his own account.
findings.acceptance_test: Either the Castle Rock story appears, labelled as his 2016 retelling of a 1995 conversation with a friend who had died, with one sentence on what it does to the control thesis; or it stays out and the resolution records why. If it goes in, the Why-not-Type-3 or unexplained section says whether deferring to Jobs fits the Type 8 reading.

findings.problem: Sayonara was first across the line in 1998 (line honours). The race's overall winner on corrected time was the 35-foot AFR Midnight Rambler. I checked this against the Wikipedia results table, which cites the organizing club's results, not against a source in the evidence record. The opened sources say "won" loosely, and Ellison uses the word himself, but a reader who knows the race will take "Sayonara won" and the FAQ's "Sayonara won the December 1998 race" as an error. Ellison also says on CNN (S09) "I had won the race in 1995," which the draft renders as "He had sailed the race in 1995."
findings.acceptance_test: Body and FAQ say Sayonara was first to finish (line honours) in 1998, checked against the race results, and neither implies it was the overall winner.

protected_passages.passage: Admired in one telling, respected in the other. It could be a slip of memory forty years on. It is also the open question about him.
protected_passages.reason: Both tellings check out against CBS and Playboy word for word. Setting them side by side is a real find, and it turns a well-worn anecdote into the question the page then tests.

protected_passages.passage: His answer to fear is to get his hands on the controls. He says nothing there about how failure would look.
protected_passages.reason: A precise reading of the 1997 quotation that stays inside what he said. It is the page's actual discriminator, stated in one line.

protected_passages.passage: That is one side of a relationship, told as a joke decades later. Louis Ellison's side is not on the record, so it stays a story Ellison tells and not a proven cause.
protected_passages.reason: Most Ellison profiles turn the father into a founding wound. This holds the line between his account and a cause, which an informed reader will trust.

protected_passages.passage: The line most attached to Ellison is that "it is not sufficient that I succeed; everyone else must fail." He says it isn't his.
protected_passages.reason: Corrects the most-repeated Ellison quotation against his own 1995 account, which I confirmed in the oral history. Few profiles get this right.

protected_passages.passage: An Eight at ease can be gentle, so some of this fits. A six-year-old afraid his mother will not come home fits every type equally. It is better left unexplained.
protected_passages.reason: Declines to bend the most affecting memory in the record to the type. Keep this even when the missing facts about his mother are added nearby.

assessment: Fan lens: the profile is unflattering in the right places, quotes its main interviews accurately, and does not reward the legend. I reopened the Smithsonian, Academy, Playboy, CBS, USC, Fortune, CNN and Kalat texts; the quotations I checked match, including both versions of the sister story and the Genghis Khan correction. The weakness is selection. Several of the best-known facts about Ellison sit in the draft's own opened sources and never reach the page, and most of them cut against the Type 8 argument or sharpen a contradiction the draft treats too gently: his first-person "like me" in the void passage, the father whose trust in government he says he rebelled against, Oracle's CIA origin, the Gates rank race, PeopleSoft, and the America's Cup. One discriminator paragraph misreads the Playboy text (fan-01). The Milken example probably omits a business partnership (fan-03, not verified in an opened source). Added together, the Type 3 alternative is argued below the strength an informed reader would bring to it, so medium confidence is the ceiling and the typing stays contested. Body length is about 3,750 words, so the additions need matching cuts. Similarity diagnostic: not tripped (maximum 0.024 against a 0.04 threshold); the listed pairs share only stock wording, and I found no reused argument. The structure and details are specific to Ellison. Limits: I did not reopen the legal, political or 2025 to 2026 deal sources, and Softwar and the Wilson biography remain unread, which is where an informed reader would look first for his first wife, co-founders and the record on embellishment.
